segments.text: Alright, let us get started, thanks for picking this room over the free coffee.
My name is Diego, I lead a small backend team, and these days a lot of our pull requests are written by AI agents.
I want to talk about how reviewing those pull requests is different, and what we changed to keep quality up.
First, a confession, for the first month we reviewed agent pull requests exactly like human ones.
That did not go well, and the reason is interesting.
When a person writes code, the size of the change roughly matches how much they thought about it.
With an agent, a twelve hundred line change can show up in four minutes, and nobody thought about all of it.
So the reviewer becomes the first person to really think about the change, and that is a lot of pressure.
The first rule we made was simple: small pull requests only, no matter who or what wrote them.
If an agent produces a big change, we ask it to split the work into steps that each make sense alone.
The second rule is that the person who started the agent owns the pull request.
They read every line before asking for review, and they answer questions about it.
You cannot say the agent did it, just like you cannot say the compiler did it.
Third, we pay a lot more attention to tests.
Agents are very good at writing tests that pass, which is not the same as tests that check anything useful.
We see tests that mock everything and then assert that the mock was called, which proves nothing.
So in review we ask one question for every test: what bug would make this fail.
If nobody can answer, the test goes.
Fourth, we look for things that are technically fine but do not fit the codebase.
A new helper that duplicates one we already have, or a second way of doing configuration.
Agents do not always know your conventions, unless you write them down where the agent can read them.
That turned out to be the most useful thing we did, honestly, we wrote our conventions down.
We keep a short file in the repo that says what we care about, and both people and agents read it.
We also use an automated reviewer that reads that same file and leaves comments on every pull request.
It catches the boring stuff, like a missing secret check or an API route that skips our usual checks.
That frees the human reviewer to think about design, which is the part that really needs a person.
Now, some patterns that show up a lot in agent code that I want you to watch for.
Defensive checks for things that cannot happen, which make code longer and hide real errors.
Comments that repeat what the code says, instead of explaining why.
Error handling that catches everything and logs it, so failures disappear quietly.
And confident looking code that calls an API method that does not exist in your version of the library.
That last one is the scariest, because it often looks right and only fails at runtime.
Type checking and running the tests in CI catches most of it, so make sure those run on every pull request.
Let me show you a real example, names changed to protect the innocent.
Here an agent added retry logic around a payment call, which looks responsible.
But the call was not idempotent, so a retry could charge someone twice.
The tests passed, the linter was happy, and only a person who knew the payment provider caught it.
That is the kind of thing human review is for now.
So, the summary: keep changes small, the person who ran the agent owns the change, and question every test.
Write your conventions down, let a bot handle the boring checks, and spend human attention on design and risk.
Thank you, that is all I have, let us take some questions.
Yeah, go ahead.
Do you worry about the cost of running all these agents and reviewers, is it actually cheaper?
So the question is whether it is actually cheaper.
Um, the model bill is small compared to salaries, the real cost is review time, which is why we keep changes small.
If review time goes up and quality goes down, it is not cheaper, so we track both.
Next, in the middle.
Do you tell reviewers which pull requests were written by an agent?
Yes, we label them, not to judge them, but because the reviewer should know to check tests more carefully.
Hi, what goes into that conventions file, like how long is it?
It is about a page, things like where config lives, how we name things, and which mistakes we never want to see again.
So, yeah, every time we find the same mistake twice in review, it goes into the file.
One more.
Has an agent ever caught something a human reviewer missed?
Yes, quite often actually, mostly small things like an unused variable or an error that was swallowed.
It is a good partner for the boring parts, and that is exactly how we use it.
Thanks everyone, enjoy the rest of the conference.
